content: Strategic information systems are designed to prevent future stock-outs by generating dashboards that display early warning indicators. These indicators alert program managers before stock shortages occur. Financial data sources, such as health expenditure data, are collected to inform national policies and for international reporting. To understand the financial context, it is essential to trace the complete flow of funds—from their source, through decision-makers, to care providers, and ultimately to the recipients of care. Health expenditure data also provide insights into what the funds are used for (e.g., salaries, commodities) and their purpose (e.g., preventive or curative care). Two international standard systems exist for tracking health spending by function, category, beneficiary, and funding source: the National AIDS Spending Assessments (NASA) and Health Accounts (HA). These systems offer the most comprehensive information on HIV/AIDS and overall health spending in many countries. Historically, countries have produced full NASAs or disease-specific subaccounts linked to general Health Accounts, including for HIV/AIDS, using the System of Health Accounts (SHA 2011) methodology. Both NASA and HIV subaccounts enable detailed reporting of expenditure categories, down to specific beneficiaries (e.g., men who have sex with men) and interventions (e.g., prevention of mother-to-child transmission, or PMTCT). In 2011, the World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with the OECD and Eurostat, introduced the SHA 2011 global standard for reporting health expenditures. This standard allows for comparisons within and across countries over time. SHA 2011 recommends fully distributing health expenditures across beneficiaries and describing them in terms of disease (e.g., HIV/AIDS), age, sex, and location. This approach provides a more rigorous technical framework by standardizing the allocation of joint expenditures, such as those for health service delivery at the facility level. Both Health Accounts with full disease distribution and NASAs are now intended to be conducted regularly. Health Accounts, including detailed disease-specific expenditures, are conducted annually or whenever more detailed information is required. NASA is a tool designed to describe financial flows and expenditures using globally standardized categories. It provides critical information on the financial gap between available and needed resources and promotes harmonization of policy tools in the HIV/AIDS field. NASA supports monitoring resource mobilization and the financial response to AIDS. It is not an accounting system but rather a mechanism for tracking spending as reported by countries. In the short term, NASA can provide data for public expenditure indicators, while in the long term, it can monitor the implementation of national strategic plans, track progress toward goals like universal access to treatment, and provide evidence of compliance with donor requirements. Health Accounts (HA) are broader in scope, tracking all health spending in a country over a defined period, regardless of the financing or managing entity. This generates consistent and comprehensive data that can inform evidence-based policymaking. HA can monitor changes in policy priorities and resource allocation following reforms or new programs. They are typically conducted annually, with provisional data available within one year and final data within two years. Starting in 2016, Health Accounts using SHA 2011 began capturing top-level elements of NASA’s AIDS spending categories annually. Revised coding and data collection tools now better track HIV/AIDS-related expenditures systematically. Nationally representative surveys, such as the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and AIDS Indicator Survey (AIS), have increasingly included HIV testing. These surveys, conducted every five years, collect data on self-reported risk behaviors, service utilization, and attitudes toward HIV-related stigma and discrimination. They provide a snapshot of HIV-related indicators and can identify service gaps and areas requiring additional resources. When repeated over time, these surveys allow for trend analysis and monitoring of progress toward national and global goals. However, in countries with low-level or concentrated epidemics, household surveys are not recommended due to challenges in reaching key populations and the large sample sizes required for representativeness. Surveys targeting key populations at higher risk for HIV infection, such as sex workers, people who inject drugs, and men who have sex with men, are essential for obtaining representative data on seroprevalence, risk behaviors, and service utilization. Integrated Bio-Behavioral Surveys (IBBS) are particularly important in countries where national strategies focus on key populations. These surveys require specialized sampling methods, such as time-location sampling (TLS) or respondent-driven sampling (RDS), to address challenges like high mobility and stigma. IBBS data inform resource allocation and priority-setting for HIV programming at the local level. Health facility surveys assess the capacity and performance of facilities in delivering care. These surveys can validate or supplement data from patient monitoring systems and administrative records. They also evaluate whether actual practices align with policies and protocols and whether providers have the necessary resources and support to deliver high-quality care. Tools like the Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) and Service Provision Assessment (SPA) surveys monitor the availability of essential resources, equipment, and services, including those related to HIV, tuberculosis, and non-communicable diseases. Vital registration systems, maintained by national governments, record births and deaths, including causes of death. These systems provide valuable epidemiological and health statistics, such as AIDS mortality rates and survival rates. However, in many lowand middle-income countries, underreporting and misclassification of causes of death limit the utility of these data for HIV monitoring and evaluation. Efforts to improve the completeness and accuracy of civil registration systems are critical for generating reliable data on HIV-related outcomes.
